question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Indian coast / waterway — its strategic significance for European powers in the 18th century]
options: Coromandel Coast (Bay of Bengal) — gateway to trade with Southeast Asia and China; key British and French contest zone
Malabar Coast (Arabian Sea) — primary source of pepper and spices; controlled access to the Arabian Sea trade routes
Cape of Good Hope (South Africa) — vital waystation on the sea route to India; controlled by the Dutch (VOC) until 1806
Strait of Hormuz — the main route used by British and French ships sailing from Europe to India via the Atlantic and Indian Ocean
wrong_fact: The Strait of Hormuz is at the mouth of the Persian Gulf and was NOT the main route used by European ships sailing from Europe to India. The primary sea route from Europe to India in the 18th century ran around the Cape of Good Hope and across the Indian Ocean — not through the Strait of Hormuz or the Persian Gulf.
explanation: European ships (British, French, Dutch, Portuguese) sailed from Europe down the Atlantic, around the Cape of Good Hope, and then northeast across the Indian Ocean to reach India's coasts. The Strait of Hormuz connects the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and was relevant only for trade within the western Indian Ocean / Persian Gulf region. The Cape of Good Hope was indeed controlled by the Dutch VOC and was a crucial waystation.

question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Indian river / port — its strategic importance in Anglo-French rivalry]
options: Hooghly River (Bengal) — served as the waterway to Calcutta and Chandernagore; both British and French had settlements on its banks
Godavari River delta — major rice-producing region whose control gave logistical advantage in the Deccan campaigns
Pondicherry harbour — natural deep-water port that gave France a major naval advantage over the British in the Bay of Bengal
Madras (Fort St. George) — primary British base on the Coromandel Coast, fell to the French in 1746
wrong_fact: Pondicherry did NOT have a natural deep-water harbour. On the contrary, Pondicherry's roadstead was notoriously shallow and exposed; it lacked a proper harbour. This was a significant strategic weakness of French India — ships had to anchor far offshore and were vulnerable during the northeast monsoon season. The British at Madras faced similar but less severe constraints.
explanation: Pondicherry's lack of a natural harbour was a key strategic disadvantage for the French. Supplies and reinforcements had to be landed through surf-boats, which was dangerous and slow. Madras was also roadstead-based but the British compensated with Calcutta (on the Hooghly) as a major river port. The Hooghly River was vital for both Calcutta and Chandernagore. Madras did fall to France's Dupleix in 1746.

question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Geographical feature / location — its strategic role in 18th-century European control of India]
options: Deccan Plateau — its fragmented political landscape (Hyderabad, Marathas, Mysore) made it a theatre of proxy wars; both Britain and France sought alliances with local powers
Northern Circars (Andhra coast) — grant of diwani over these territories by the Mughal emperor to the French in 1753 gave France a revenue base north of Madras
Mauritius (Île de France) — French naval base in the Indian Ocean used to threaten British shipping and support operations in India
Ceylon (Sri Lanka) — held by the Dutch throughout the 18th century and transferred to Britain in 1796 during the French Revolutionary Wars
wrong_fact: The Northern Circars were NOT granted to France by the Mughal emperor. The Northern Circars (five districts along the Andhra coast) were granted as a jagir (mansabdari grant) to the French general Bussy by the Nizam of Hyderabad in 1753 — not by the Mughal emperor. The Mughal emperor had by this time very limited effective authority over such regions.
explanation: Bussy-Castelnau secured the Northern Circars from Salabat Jung (the Nizam of Hyderabad) in 1753 as payment for French military support. This gave France control of a rich coastal strip north of Madras and a significant revenue base. It was not a Mughal imperial grant. The British later wrested the Northern Circars (Warren Hastings secured them from the Nizam in 1765–1766). Mauritius (Île de France) was indeed a key French naval base, and Ceylon was Dutch until 1796.
